problem: The sentence says that if the receiver samples late it may read the tail of the previous slot or the start of the next slot. This contradicts the quiz Q4 answer and is technically wrong: a late sample drifts forward into the start of the next slot, while reading the tail of the previous slot happens when the sample is early.
fix: If the receiver samples early, it may read the tail of the previous slot; if it samples late, it may read the start of the next slot. Guard time reduces this.

problem: 'Frame slip' is used for a one-slot misalignment that swaps channel 1 into channel 2. In standard telephony a frame slip means a whole frame is lost or repeated because the receiver clock drifts from the incoming clock.
fix: If sync is lost, the receiver may slip by one slot and route channel 1 into channel 2; this is a slot slip (loss of frame alignment). A frame slip is the loss or repetition of a whole frame when the receiver clock drifts.

problem: 'A sync bit in every frame is enough for four channels' is an unsupported claim; the risk of false locking depends on the data pattern and sync pattern, not on the number of channels being four.
fix: A single sync bit per frame is a weak marker, because a data bit in the same position can look like sync. Many systems therefore use a longer sync word, sent every frame or spread over a multiframe, to avoid false locking.

problem: 'Some syllabi write TDM(A) for that access method' reads as if the abbreviation is TDM(A); the intended term is TDMA.
fix: TDMA is multiple access, where users take turns on a shared radio channel. Some syllabi write TDMA for that access method.

problem: '125×10-6 s' has no superscript, so a student can read it as 125 times minus six seconds.
